# 28 — Draft Core: Abstract, Contributions, Results

**Date:** 2026-07-24
**Status:** DRAFT PROSE. Every number here is generated by
`src/pneuma_lab/audit/table.py` from the coded corpus and pinned by regression tests
in `tests/research/test_audit_table.py`. If a number in the paper disagrees with the
generator, the generator is right.

---

## Abstract

Papers reporting that persistent memory improves an LLM agent describe their evaluations
in terms of items: two thousand questions, a thousand tasks, a hundred human ratings.
Those items are not independent. The two thousand questions are drawn from ten
conversations; the thousand tasks from five websites; the hundred ratings from a single
simulation run. We audit thirty published agent-memory systems and benchmarks against a
rubric frozen before coding, and compute what effect size each design could have detected
across a range of clustering assumptions. Thirteen of thirty-two coded rows cannot be
bounded at all, because the paper does not state the count of its own coarsest grouping.
Only six state an effect precisely enough to compare against any threshold, and five of
those six fall below it at every clustering assumption we report. We further distinguish
two kinds of dependence that the existing power literature does not model, because they
are created by the intervention rather than by the data: a memory pool that accumulates
across an evaluation couples every task to its predecessors, and a single induced artifact
scored on thousands of items provides one replication of the claim about that artifact,
not thousands. We report our own prior work under the identical rubric, where it records
the worst overstatement ratio in the frame.

---

## Contributions, as they should appear in §1

1. **An audit.** Thirty agent-memory systems and benchmarks coded against a rubric frozen
   before any paper was read, with every non-numeric cell backed by a verbatim quote and
   the full coding sheet released.
2. **A taxonomy.** Three kinds of dependence, two of which are absent from the existing
   power and clustering literature because they arise from the intervention under test
   rather than from the benchmark.
3. **A detectability surface.** Per paper, the minimum detectable effect across a grid of
   intraclass correlation and paired discordance, reported as a range and never as a point,
   with verdict stability stated explicitly.
4. **A released tool** that takes a reported design and returns that surface.

**What we do not claim**, stated in the same paragraph: we do not claim any audited system
fails to work; we do not estimate effective sample size, which published cluster counts do
not identify; and the detectability method is not ours — it is Card et al.'s, applied to a
literature that has a structural reason to need it.

## §5 Results — the numbers, verbatim from the generator

### 5.1 Most claims cannot be checked at all

Of 32 coded rows:

|                                                                  |  count |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | -----: |
| Non-identifiable — no stated grouping count, or a single cluster | **13** |
| Identifiable but stating no verifiable absolute effect           | **13** |
| **Verdict-eligible**                                             |  **6** |

Four distinct reasons a row is not checkable, each observed:

- **No magnitude stated.** MemoryBank and Think-in-Memory both assert improvement in prose
  without ever giving a number.
- **No unit count stated.** Seven papers — A-MEM, SWE-Exp, AgeMem, MemoryOS, G-Memory,
  MemGPT's headline result, and MemBench's evaluated subset — never report the count of
  their own coarsest grouping.
- **Relative stated as absolute.** ASI reports "23.5% and 11.3% in success rate"; the
  arithmetic identifies these as relative, and the absolute values are 7.7 and 4.1.
- **Magnitude not recomputable.** Reflexion states "an absolute 22%"; two independent
  attempts could not reproduce it from the paper's own reported quantities.

A fifth, distinct from all four: **budget-mismatched comparison.** JARVIS-1's "5 times"
pairs its own 60-minute result against a baseline's 20-minute result. The paper reports
that baseline at 60 minutes itself, where the ratio is 4.17.

### 5.2 Of the claims that can be checked, most fall below their own threshold

| Paper                 | Claim (pp) | MDE range (pp) | Verdict          |
| --------------------- | ---------: | -------------- | ---------------- |
| Zep (DMR arm)         |        0.4 | 4.8 – 7.9      | **stable below** |
| Agent Skill Induction |        7.7 | 11.5 – 79.2    | **stable below** |
| ReasoningBank         |        8.3 | 12.8 – 88.6    | **stable below** |
| Agent Workflow Memory |       12.0 | 11.5 – 79.2    | flips            |
| ExpeL                 |       19.0 | 16.7 – 102.3   | flips            |
| Reflexion             |       22.0 | 9.4 – 15.3     | stable above     |

At the reference discordance, **five of six fall below their own detection threshold at
every intraclass correlation on the grid.** Three of those hold across the entire
two-dimensional surface. The single claim that clears its threshold everywhere, Reflexion,
is also the only one of the six whose design has no clustering at all — its 134 tasks come
from 134 environments. That is what the taxonomy predicts.

### 5.3 Reporting practice

|                                        | count of 32 |
| -------------------------------------- | ----------: |
| No pre-specified decision rule         |      **31** |
| No inert-content null arm              |      **28** |
| Uncertainty over the coarsest grouping |       **0** |

The single row coding anything other than `none` on a pre-specified decision rule is our
own, which was preregistered. AgentCL is the only paper reporting an interval at all, and
each of its confidence intervals sits inside one task stream, so it structurally cannot
resample the unit it would need to.

### 5.4 Our own result, under the identical rubric

E-0 reports 3,141 evaluation instances drawn from 4 repositories — an overstatement ratio
of **785.2, the highest in the frame**, nearly four times Mem0's 200.0. Its reported
statistic, $z = -16.03$, is computed over items; clustering by repository deflates it to
2.53 at $\rho=0.05$ and 0.57 at $\rho=1$.

The direction matters. E-0's verdict was a failure — our own system lost to a retry-count
controller — so item-level inference inflated our confidence in a **negative** result. At
defensible clustering we could not have concluded that either. The same error inflates
nulls as readily as positives, and an audit applying its critique only to favourable
findings would be practising the selective rigour it documents.

---

## Two sentences the paper must contain

> We do not claim that any audited system fails to work. We claim that most of these
> studies could not have detected the effects they report, and that a majority do not
> report enough for a reader to check.

> The detectability method is not ours. What is ours is the observation that an
> agent-memory system is, by construction, the mechanism that destroys the independence of
> its own evaluation — and that the stronger the memory effect, the more severe the
> violation of the assumption used to test it.
